170
Distribution on LHI: Upper slopes and summits of Mt Lidgbird and Mt Gower.
Total distribution: Circumglobal in the tropics and subtropics.
Discussion: This species has not been reported previously from Lord Howe Island. However,
there are several collections in Australian herbaria, identified by Dr Christine Cargill, dating
back to 1978. It is surprising that there are no collections before that date, as it is an easily
recognisable species and on Lord Howe Island seems to be quite common on easily reachable
branches of trees in montane forests. This raises the possibility that it has either arrived recently
on the island or spread from previously unreachable areas on the island.
Hasegawa (1984) suggested that Dendroceros japonicus from Japan might be closely allied and
perhaps conspecific with D. borbonicus and D. granulatus, the latter having a distribution from
Indonesia to the western Pacific, including Queensland and New Zealand. Furthermore, Garcia
et al. (2010) noted that Hasegawa, in unpublished notes, suggested that Dendroceros crispatus
is closely related to D. granulatus.
Campbell (1986) described D. granulatus from New Zealand material, and her description does
agree well with specimens of D. crispatus from Queensland and Lord Howe Island. Duff et al.
(2007) considered that Dendroceros subgenus Dendroceros separated into two clades (one
containing D. granulatus and D. crispatus and the other containing D. crispus of the Americas)
on morphological grounds, supported by a single-locus chlDNA (rbcL) phylogeny. However,
there appears to be enough difference at this single locus to warrant maintaining D. granulatus
as distinct from D. crispatus, at least until a more detailed molecular analysis can be made.

Megaceros Campb.
This genus is found only in Oceania and southern and South East Asia, and comprises about 17
validly published species (Tropicos 2016), of which three are currently accepted for Australia
(Cargill et al. 2013). One species occurs on Lord Howe Island.

Megaceros gracilis (Reichardt) Steph.
Anthoceros gracilis Reichardt, Verh. Zool.-Bot. Ges. Wien 16: 957 (1866); Megaceros gracilis
(Reichardt) Steph., Sp. Hepat. 4: 955 (1916)
Type: AUSTRALIA, New South Wales, Sydney, Jelinek s.n., s.d. [Nov–Dec 1858], holotype,
not extant; New South Wales, Clyde Mountain, Curnow and Lepp 4198, 25 Aug 1991, neotype
CBG-9501586!, isoneotypes AK, MEL, NSW (not seen).
Description: This species was described by Scott (1985) and in more detail by Cargill et al.
(2013).
Illustrations: Scott (1985, Figure 4); Cargill et al. (2013, Figure 5).
Habitat: On soil, rock or rotting wood in damp or wet situations, usually along watercourses.
Distribution on LHI: Central and southern areas, along permanent streams.
Total distribution: Australia (Tas, ACT, NSW, Qld, LHI), Malesia, Papua New Guinea, New
Caledonia, islands of the Pacific.
Discussion: This species was reported from Lord Howe Island only recently, by Cargill et al.
(2013). However, there are numerous collections from the island in Australian herbaria,
identified by Dr Christine Cargill, dating back to at least the 1960s. The fact that this very
noticeable species was not collected earlier on the island by William Watts in 1911 suggests that
it may have been introduced, or has spread from previously unreachable areas of the island.

                                                 171
The original type was collected in Sydney by Anton Jelinek, botanist (with Eduard Schwarz) on
the Austrian Novara expedition which was in Sydney during November and December 1858.
However, Cargill et al. (2013) noted that the type is apparently no longer extant, and therefore
selected a neotype.
From their molecular results based on a combined ITS-2, rbcL and trnL–trnF analysis, Cargill
et al. (2013) concluded that Megaceros from Australia, Lord Howe Island and New Caledonia
forms a clade containing two cryptic species that cannot be distinguished morphologically. They
therefore chose to retain the name Megaceros gracilis for all Australian plants that are not
monoicous and have spores without a reticulated pattern.


Notothyladaceae (Milde) Müll. Frib. ex Prosk.
The family Notothyladaceae is the second-largest of the hornwort families, comprising about 60
species in three genera (Villarreal et al. 2010a). The treatment for the Flora of Australia project
is still in preparation, so the taxonomy and other aspects presented here may change once that
treatment is completed.

Phaeoceros Prosk.
Phaeoceros Prosk, Bull. Torrey Bot. Club 78: 346 (1951)
This world-wide genus comprises about 40 species (Villarreal et al. 2010b), of which four are
currently known from Australia (Cargill and Fuhrer 2008), two from New Caledonia
(Thouvenot et al. 2011) and two from New Zealand (Glenny 1998). Two New Zealand species
previously included in Phaeoceros were transferred to Phaeomegaceros by Duff et al. (2007).
One species of Phaeoceros occurs on Lord Howe Island.

seen.
Description: This species was described in detail by Cargill and Fuhrer (2008).
Illustration: Cargill and Fuhrer (2008, Figures 1–2).
Habitat on LHI: Wet soil, rock and rotting wood.
Distribution on LHI: Southern half of the island, in or near creeklines.
Total distribution: Circumglobal.

Aneura alterniloba Aneuraceae                                                WSTVAN
This is one of the commonest of the thallose liverworts, occurring in all wet forests
and also in riparian habitats in drier areas, where it can be immersed in water. The
thallus is irregularly pinnate and about 3 to 6 mm wide. The apices are deeply dissected
and almost always bent slightly downwards. Capsules, which are rare, are long,
enclosed in a thick, tubular shoot-calyptra 5 to 8 mm long.
     A. rodwayi (TVN) is a smaller species with the margins curved upwards, so
that in cross-section the thallus is concave. It has been reported from very different
habitats, including coastal limestone cliffs and alpine bogs. We suspect that not all
records are accurate. A. stolonifera (T) we have never seen.

Similar species: Megaceros gracilis, Phaeoceros spp., Riccardia spp.




Asterel/a drummondii Aytoniaceae                                               WSTVAN
 This is probably the commonest of the thallose liverworts in very dry habitats, and it
is also quite common in wet regions. The solid but rather brittle thallus is 5 to 7 mm
wide, and (excephn drier habitats) usually forked laterally into two or sometimes
 more tongue-like lobes. The 1orsal surface is usually green, but the margins and
ventral surface (and also sometimes the dorsal surface) are distinctly crimson-black.
When dry the thallus folds up along its length, and when it is quite dry only the dark,
 wavy edges of the ventral surface are exposed. The pseudoperianths, which hang
from a tall archegoniophore, are each adorned with a frill of 12 to 14 white strips
joined at the tips. When squashed, the thallus has an unusual fisliy smell.
    A. tenera (VT) is a much smaller species, the thallus rarely more than 4 mm wide.
The pseudoperianths have no more than 10 strips, which become separated at the
tips. Wf; have not seen A. tasmanica (T) or A. whiteleggei (N).
    Reboulia queenslandica (WS'.fVN) is rather similar in size, but the air pores on
the dorsal surface are more obvio_us and are surrounded by four or five concentric
rings of cells. The thallus consists mostly of spongy tissue filled with air chambers, a
fact that can be observed under a hand lens if a thallus is cut in half. Records of
R. hemisphaerica 1n the region are this species.

Similar species: Plagiochasma rupestre, Targionia lorbeeriana

---

This genus of large thallose liverworts is well known to horticulturalists, because
the species thrive in gardens and greenhouses. Only Lunularia cruciata can be
confused with the following species, and then only when gemmae cups are absent.
The other obvious characteristic is the pres_ence of polygonal zones on the upper
surface of the thallus, each zone having a central pore leading to an air-chamber
below. The gemmae cups are circular and crown-like. The archegoniophore is also
characteristic, producing radial rows of pendent yellow capsules alternating with
sterile photosynthetic rays.

M. berteroana                                                                    WSTVAN
This species is common in grassy bogs, but is also found on the banks of streams and
other damp places. The dorsal surface is a shiny pale green and, characteristically, the
v�ntral surface is covered by pale, almost transparent scales which extend
more-or­less to the margins. Gemmae cups are usually present, except in very humid
habitats. They have toothed and slightly hairy margins, and the gemmae within
are bright green arid discus-shaped.
M. foliacea                                                                          TVAN
This is often confused with M berteroana, but the ventral scales are crimson and are
restricted to a narrow strip close to the centreline of the ventral surface of the thallus.
The archegoniophore is flat, so that the head looks like an indented disc.

M.polymorpha                                                                    TVAN
An introduction from Europe, this species is easily recognised by the dark streak or
groove down the middle of the upper surface of the thallus. When growing in a
greenhouse or permanently moist habitat, the thallus is usually larger than the other
two species and is a duller green.

Similar specie]: Lunularia cruciata


 Megaceros gracilis Dendrocerotaceae                                                 TVAN
The fleshy, dark green thallus of this homwort is very similar to that of Phaeoceros
species, but there are often Nostoc c�vities embedded in the thallus, close to the surface.
The margins are irregularly lobed and also finely toothed or ragged, unlike the smooth
margins in Phaeoceros. A further distinction is in the number of chloroplasts per
cell: 2 in this species, but only I in I:!Jaeoceros. Capsules are typical ofthe hornworts,
long and needle-like, arising from a thick basal collar. the spores.appear green because
they contain chloroplasts, but the spore wall is actually colourless or grey.

Similar species: Anthoceros spp., Phaeoceros spp.

Metzgeria decipiens Metzgeriaceae                                            WfVAN
Metzgeria species are common epiphytes in forests, and are particul�rly common in
rainforest an_d fern gullies. M. decipiens is probably the most common in the region.
The narrow, Y..branched shoots, never more than 2 mm wide, lie flat against the bark
or creep over other bryophytes, forming open, yellow-green to wefts that often overlap.
There is a narrow but distinct midrib in each lobe, separating the two thin wings.
There are usually at least a few hairs on the margins and ventral surface, including
the midrib.
     M. australis (TV) has the marginal hairs usually paired (in M. decipiens this
 condition is uncommon), but is otherwise much the same.
     M. furcata (TVAN) is almost indistinguishable from M. decipiens in the f ield,
,the major difference being in the number of cells overlying the midrib. It sometimes
 produces many gemmae, like miniature thalli, from the side margins. It is more likely
 to be found on rocks than is decipiens. M. densiseta (TVAN) is very similar but lacks
 gemmae and has a narrower thallus (to about 1 mm).
     M. leptoneura (TVN) - M. hamata of Scott (1985) - has a narrow thallus (to
p � wide) with the margins inrolled slightly, and the hairs on the margins and
ventral midrib are mostly falcate. M. grollei is the same species.
     M. saccata (TVN) has the thallus rolled up to form a series of sacs, only 1 mm
wide or even less. It seems to be extremely rare. M atrichoneura (TV) also has
the thallus rolled up, but it is even smaller than M. saccata - just 0.5 mm wide. It
produces many gemmae from the side margins, the gemmae thus appearing to be
ventral because of the inrolling of the thallus. M. hispidissima (TV) has dense hairs
on both ventral and dorsal surfaces. It is very rare in the region.

Similar species: other Metzgeria spp.
